{{external media | width = 210px | float = right | headerimage= | video1 = [https://knowablemagazine.org/article/living-world/2020/beat-life-understanding-cells-rhythms "Beat of life: Understanding the cell's rhythms"], Michael Elowitz on cellular oscillations, ''[[Knowable Magazine]]'' }}

'''Michael B. Elowitz''' is a [[biologist]] and professor of Biology, Bioengineering, and Applied Physics at the [[California Institute of Technology]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.elowitz.caltech.edu/people.html|title=The Elowitz Lab [Caltech]|website=www.elowitz.caltech.edu}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://biology.caltech.edu/Members/Elowitz |title=Biology Division - Michael Elowitz |access-date=March 27, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100624171119/http://biology.caltech.edu/Members/Elowitz |archive-date=June 24, 2010 |df=dmy-all }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.aph.caltech.edu/people/elowitz_m.html|title=Caltech Applied Physics - Not Found|website=www.aph.caltech.edu}}</ref> and investigator at the [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.hhmi.org/news/elowitz_bio.html|title=Michael B. Elowitz, PhD - HHMI.org}}</ref> In 2007 he was the recipient of a [[MacArthur Fellowship]] for the design of a synthetic [[gene regulatory network]], the [[Repressilator]], which helped initiate the field of [[synthetic biology]].<ref>{{cite journal|title=Ten years of synergy|date=January 1, 2010|journal=Nature|volume=463|issue=7279|pages=269–270|doi=10.1038/463269b|pmid=20090703|bibcode=2010Natur.463R.269.|doi-access=free}}</ref> He was the first to show how inherently random effects, or 'noise', in gene expression could be detected and quantified in living cells,<ref>{{cite journal|url=http://stke.sciencemag.org/cgi/content/abstract/sci;297/5584/1183|title=Database of Cell Signaling and Virtual Journal - Science Signaling|journal=Science|date=August 16, 2002 |volume=297 |issue=5584 |pages=1183–1186 |doi=10.1126/science.1070919 |last1=Elowitz |first1=Michael B. |last2=Levine |first2=Arnold J. |last3=Siggia |first3=Eric D. |last4=Swain |first4=Peter S. |pmid=12183631 |bibcode=2002Sci...297.1183E |url-access=subscription }}</ref> leading to a growing recognition of the many roles that noise plays in living cells. His work in Synthetic Biology and Noise represent two foundations of the field of Systems Biology. Since then, his laboratory has contributed to the development of synthetic biological circuits that perform a range of functions inside cells, and revealed biological circuit design principles underlying epigenetic memory, cell fate control, cell-cell communication, and multicellular behaviors.<ref>{{cite web |title=Elowitz lab website |url=https://www.elowitz.caltech.edu/}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Elowitz was born in [[Los Angeles|Los Angeles, California]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Michael Elowitz |url=https://www.macfound.org/fellows/class-of-2007/michael-elowitz |access-date=2026-01-07 |website=www.macfound.org |language=en}}</ref> where he attended the Portola Highly Gifted Magnet School and the [[Hamilton Humanities Magnet High Schools]]. In 1992, he received his B.A. in physics from the [[University of California, Berkeley]]. In 1999, he completed his Ph.D. in physics at [[Princeton University]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Michael B. Elowitz - Biology and Biological Engineering |url=https://www.bbe.caltech.edu/people/michael-b-elowitz |access-date=2026-01-07 |website=www.bbe.caltech.edu}}</ref>

As a graduate student under the mentorship of [[Stanislas Leibler]], he began designing synthetic genetic circuits [https://paw.princeton.edu/article/michael-b-elowitz-99-researches-how-cells-change-over-time]. During his graduate studies, he spent a year at the European Molecular Biology Laboratory (EMBL) in Heidelberg, where he engineered parts of the [[Repressilator]]. Upon returning to Princeton, Elowitz showed that the circuit could successfully generate dynamic oscillations in gene expression, causing individual cells to "blink" on and off, and demonstrating that new dynamic behaviors could be programmed in living cells.<ref name="nature.com">{{Cite journal |last1=Elowitz |first1=Michael B. |last2=Leibler |first2=Stanislas |date=January 2000 |title=A synthetic oscillatory network of transcriptional regulators |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/35002125 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=403 |issue=6767 |pages=335–338 |doi=10.1038/35002125 |pmid=10659856 |bibcode=2000Natur.403..335E |issn=1476-4687}}</ref>

==Career==
His laboratory studies the dynamics of genetic circuits in individual living cells using synthetic biology, time-lapse microscopy, and mathematical modeling, with a particular focus on the way in which cells make use of noise to implement behaviors that would be difficult or impossible without it. Recently, his lab has expanded their approaches beyond bacteria to include eukaryotic and mammalian cells.<ref>[http://www.hhmi.org/research/investigators/elowitz.html "Gene Circuit Dynamics in Regulation and Differentiation", ''Howard Hughes Medical Institute'']</ref>

== Research ==
Elowitz's research seeks to learn how to program new behaviors in living cells through a "build to understand" approach.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Elowitz |first1=Michael |last2=Lim |first2=Wendell A. |date=December 2010 |title=Build life to understand it |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=468 |issue=7326 |pages=889–890 |doi=10.1038/468889a |pmid=21164460 |pmc=3068207 |bibcode=2010Natur.468..889E |issn=1476-4687}}</ref> His laboratory integrates synthetic biology, quantitative systems biology, and single-cell analysis techniques. Lab research has focused on biological circuits that process and store information, allow cell-cell communication, generate differentiation and other dynamic cell behaviors, as well as circuits that can provide therapeutic capabilities.<ref name=Lu>{{Cite bioRxiv | last1=Lu | first1=Andrew | last2=Moeller | first2=Lukas | last3=Moore | first3=Stephen | last4=Xia | first4=Shiyu | last5=Ho | first5=Kevin | last6=Zhang | first6=Evan | last7=Budde | first7=Mark W. | last8=Larson | first8=Haley | last9=Ahmed Diaz | first9=Ali | last10=Gu | first10=Bo | last11=Linton | first11=James M. | last12=Klock | first12=Leslie | last13=Flynn | first13=Michael J. | last14=Gao | first14=Xiaojing J. | last15=Siegwart | first15=Daniel J. | last16=Zhu | first16=Hao | last17=Elowitz | first17=Michael B. | title=Engineered protein circuits for cancer therapy | date=2025 | biorxiv=10.1101/2025.04.16.647665 }}</ref><ref name=Flynn>{{Cite bioRxiv |last1=Flynn |first1=Michael J. |last2=Mayfield |first2=Acacia M. H. |last3=Du |first3=Rongrong |last4=Gradinaru |first4=Viviana |last5=Elowitz |first5=Michael B. |date=2024-03-14 |title=Synthetic dosage-compensating miRNA circuits allow precision gene therapy for Rett syndrome |biorxiv=10.1101/2024.03.13.584179 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Du |first1=Rongrong |last2=Flynn |first2=Michael J. |last3=Mahe |first3=Karan |last4=Honsa |first4=Monique |last5=Gu |first5=Bo |last6=Li |first6=Dongyang |last7=McGeary |first7=Sean E. |last8=Gradinaru |first8=Viviana |last9=Jungmann |first9=Ralf |last10=Elowitz |first10=Michael B. |title=MiRNA modules for precise, tunable control of gene expression |journal=Molecular Cell |date=2026 |volume=86 |issue=1 |pages=194–212.e7 |doi=10.1016/j.molcel.2025.11.028 |pmid=41421338 |biorxiv=10.1101/2024.03.12.583048 }}</ref>

=== The repressilator ===
As a graduate student, Elowitz designed and constructed the repressilator, a synthetic genetic oscillator composed of three transcriptional repressors arranged in a cyclic inhibitory loop. This fully synthetic circuit, rationally designed using mathematical modeling, generated periodic fluorescence oscillations in individual cells, demonstrating that engineered gene networks can produce predictable dynamic behaviors.<ref name="nature.com"/> Together with a simultaneous demonstration of synthetic toggle switches, this work sparked the development of synthetic biology.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cameron |first1=D. Ewen |last2=Bashor |first2=Caleb J. |last3=Collins |first3=James J. |date=May 2014 |title=A brief history of synthetic biology |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nrmicro3239 |journal=Nature Reviews Microbiology |language=en |volume=12 |issue=5 |pages=381–390 |doi=10.1038/nrmicro3239 |pmid=24686414 |issn=1740-1534}}</ref>

=== Stochastic gene expression and its functional roles ===
A major theme of Elowitz's work has been quantifying how stochastic biochemical events lead to both useful and deleterious biological variation. In 2002, his group introduced two fluorescent reporters into the same cells, enabling them to quantify intrinsic stochastic noise in gene expression from other, extrinsic, sources of variation, such as fluctuations in upstream components.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Elowitz |first1=Michael B. |last2=Levine |first2=Arnold J. |last3=Siggia |first3=Eric D. |last4=Swain |first4=Peter S. |date=2002-08-16 |title=Stochastic Gene Expression in a Single Cell |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1070919 |journal=Science |volume=297 |issue=5584 |pages=1183–1186 |doi=10.1126/science.1070919 |pmid=12183631 |bibcode=2002Sci...297.1183E }}</ref> Subsequent time-lapse studies showed that intrinsic and extrinsic noise operate on distinct timescales,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rosenfeld |first1=Nitzan |last2=Young |first2=Jonathan W. |last3=Alon |first3=Uri |last4=Swain |first4=Peter S. |last5=Elowitz |first5=Michael B. |date=2005-03-25 |title=Gene Regulation at the Single-Cell Level |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1106914 |journal=Science |volume=307 |issue=5717 |pages=1962–1965 |doi=10.1126/science.1106914 |pmid=15790856 |bibcode=2005Sci...307.1962R }}</ref> and showed that correlations in stochastic fluctuations can be used to infer molecular interactions in synthetic and natural circuits.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dunlop |first1=Mary J. |last2=Cox |first2=Robert Sidney |last3=Levine |first3=Joseph H. |last4=Murray |first4=Richard M. |last5=Elowitz |first5=Michael B. |date=December 2008 |title=Regulatory activity revealed by dynamic correlations in gene expression noise |journal=Nature Genetics |language=en |volume=40 |issue=12 |pages=1493–1498 |doi=10.1038/ng.281 |pmid=19029898 |pmc=2829635 |issn=1546-1718}}</ref>

Elowitz's lab also revealed functional roles for noise. For example, they showed how excitable gene-circuit architectures generate probabilistic, rather than deterministic, differentiation behaviors to enable bet-hedging in prokaryotes.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Eldar |first1=Avigdor |last2=Elowitz |first2=Michael B. |date=September 2010 |title=Functional roles for noise in genetic circuits |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=467 |issue=7312 |pages=167–173 |doi=10.1038/nature09326 |pmid=20829787 |pmc=4100692 |bibcode=2010Natur.467..167E |issn=1476-4687}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Süel |first1=Gürol M. |last2=Kulkarni |first2=Rajan P. |last3=Dworkin |first3=Jonathan |last4=Garcia-Ojalvo |first4=Jordi |last5=Elowitz |first5=Michael B. |date=2007-03-23 |title=Tunability and Noise Dependence in Differentiation Dynamics |url=https://www.science.org/doi/abs/10.1126/science.1137455 |journal=Science |volume=315 |issue=5819 |pages=1716–1719 |doi=10.1126/science.1137455 |pmid=17379809 |bibcode=2007Sci...315.1716S }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Süel |first1=Gürol M. |last2=Garcia-Ojalvo |first2=Jordi |last3=Liberman |first3=Louisa M. |last4=Elowitz |first4=Michael B. |date=March 2006 |title=An excitable gene regulatory circuit induces transient cellular differentiation |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nature04588 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=440 |issue=7083 |pages=545–550 |doi=10.1038/nature04588 |pmid=16554821 |bibcode=2006Natur.440..545S |issn=1476-4687}}</ref> In a different study, Elowitz and his team showed how noise in bacterial sporulation could facilitate developmental evolution by enabling partially penetrant mutant phenotypes.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2009-07-20 |title=Michael Elowitz and Avigdor Eldar Show How Evolution Can Allow for Large Developmental Leaps |url=http://www.aphms.caltech.edu/news/michael-elowitz-and-avigdor-eldar-show-how-evolution-can-allow-for-large-developmental-leaps |access-date=2026-01-13 |website=Applied Physics and Materials Science |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Eldar |first1=Avigdor |last2=Chary |first2=Vasant K. |last3=Xenopoulos |first3=Panagiotis |last4=Fontes |first4=Michelle E. |last5=Losón |first5=Oliver C. |last6=Dworkin |first6=Jonathan |last7=Piggot |first7=Patrick J. |last8=Elowitz |first8=Michael B. |date=July 2009 |title=Partial penetrance facilitates developmental evolution in bacteria |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=460 |issue=7254 |pages=510–514 |doi=10.1038/nature08150 |pmid=19578359 |pmc=2716064 |bibcode=2009Natur.460..510E |issn=1476-4687}}</ref>

Extending this approach to mammalian cells, he worked with [[Ellen Rothenberg (scientist)|Ellen Rothenberg]] to show that stochastic epigenetic events at a single gene could control [[T cell]] lineage commitment.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ng |first1=Kenneth KH |last2=Yui |first2=Mary A. |last3=Mehta |first3=Arnav |last4=Siu |first4=Sharmayne |last5=Irwin |first5=Blythe |last6=Pease |first6=Shirley |last7=Hirose |first7=Satoshi |last8=Elowitz |first8=Michael B. |last9=Rothenberg |first9=Ellen V. |last10=Kueh |first10=Hao Yuan |title=A stochastic epigenetic switch controls the dynamics of T-cell lineage commitment |journal=eLife |date=2018 |volume=7 |article-number=e37851 |doi=10.7554/eLife.37851 |doi-access=free |pmid=30457103 |pmc=6245732 }}</ref> Collectively, this and other work established that stochastic interactions can control cellular decision-making.

=== Pulsing, dynamics, and time-based regulation ===
Building on these discoveries, Elowitz's group went on to discover an inherently dynamic mode of gene regulation, in which transcription factors regulate genes through dynamic pulsing rather than through steady activation levels. In these systems, cells control the frequency and relative timing of activity pulses rather than tune steady-state factor activities. In yeast, they showed that the Crz1 transcription factor undergoes frequency-modulated nuclear localization bursts whose rate encodes upstream input signals, enabling cells to coordinate the responses of many genes.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cai |first1=Long |last2=Dalal |first2=Chiraj K. |last3=Elowitz |first3=Michael B. |date=September 2008 |title=Frequency-modulated nuclear localization bursts coordinate gene regulation |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=455 |issue=7212 |pages=485–490 |doi=10.1038/nature07292 |pmid=18818649 |pmc=2695983 |bibcode=2008Natur.455..485C |issn=1476-4687}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2008-09-30 |title=Caltech Scientists Find Cells Coordinate Gene Activity with FM Bursts |url=http://www.bbe.caltech.edu/news/caltech-scientists-find-cells-coordinate-gene-activity-fm-bursts-1470 |access-date=2026-01-14 |website=CaltechBBE |language=en}}</ref> They then demonstrated that cells use the relative timing of pulses to integrate information from multiple signaling pathways.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lin |first1=Yihan |last2=Sohn |first2=Chang Ho |last3=Dalal |first3=Chiraj K. |last4=Cai |first4=Long |last5=Elowitz |first5=Michael B. |date=November 2015 |title=Combinatorial gene regulation by modulation of relative pulse timing |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=527 |issue=7576 |pages=54–58 |doi=10.1038/nature15710 |pmid=26466562 |pmc=4870307 |bibcode=2015Natur.527...54L |issn=1476-4687}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-10-21 |title=Cells Rhythmically Regulate Their Genes |url=https://www.caltech.edu/about/news/cells-rhythmically-regulate-their-genes-48527 |access-date=2026-01-14 |website=California Institute of Technology |language=en}}</ref> Interestingly, pulsatile regulation was not limited to eukaryotes. Elowitz's team showed that bacteria generate dynamic pulses of the sigma factors regulating the general stress response.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Locke |first1=James C. W. |last2=Young |first2=Jonathan W. |last3=Fontes |first3=Michelle |last4=Jiménez |first4=María Jesús Hernández |last5=Elowitz |first5=Michael B. |date=2011-10-21 |title=Stochastic Pulse Regulation in Bacterial Stress Response |journal=Science |volume=334 |issue=6054 |pages=366–369 |doi=10.1126/science.1208144 |pmc=4100694 |pmid=21979936 |bibcode=2011Sci...334..366L }}</ref> Collectively, this work revealed a pervasive, inherently dynamic mode of gene regulation, its mechanistic basis, and its functional roles.

=== Discovery of eukaryotic circuit design principles ===
Moving from gene regulation to cell-cell communication, Elowitz's laboratory uncovered principles of important signaling pathways. His group discovered that interactions between Notch receptors and ligands in the same cell (cis interactions) can generate mutually exclusive "sender" and "receiver" states<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sprinzak |first1=David |last2=Lakhanpal |first2=Amit |last3=LeBon |first3=Lauren |last4=Santat |first4=Leah A. |last5=Fontes |first5=Michelle E. |last6=Anderson |first6=Graham A. |last7=Garcia-Ojalvo |first7=Jordi |last8=Elowitz |first8=Michael B. |date=May 2010 |title=Cis-interactions between Notch and Delta generate mutually exclusive signalling states |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=465 |issue=7294 |pages=86–90 |doi=10.1038/nature08959 |pmid=20418862 |pmc=2886601 |bibcode=2010Natur.465...86S |issn=1476-4687}}</ref> or allow autocrine signaling.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nandagopal |first1=Nagarajan |last2=Santat |first2=Leah A |last3=Elowitz |first3=Michael B |date=2019-01-10 |title=Cis-activation in the Notch signaling pathway |journal=eLife |language=en |volume=8 |article-number=e37880 |doi=10.7554/eLife.37880 |doi-access=free |pmid=30628888 |pmc=6345567 |issn=2050-084X }}</ref> They further discovered that different Notch ligands can activate distinct transcriptional programs through a single receptor by activating it with different dynamics, showing how signaling pathways use dynamics to encode and decode information.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nandagopal |first1=Nagarajan |last2=Santat |first2=Leah A. |last3=LeBon |first3=Lauren |last4=Sprinzak |first4=David |last5=Bronner |first5=Marianne E. |last6=Elowitz |first6=Michael B. |date=2018-02-08 |title=Dynamic Ligand Discrimination in the Notch Signaling Pathway |journal=Cell |language=en |volume=172 |issue=4 |pages=869–880.e19 |doi=10.1016/j.cell.2018.01.002 |issn=0092-8674 |pmid=29398116 |pmc=6414217 }}</ref>

Extending this work to spatial patterning, Elowitz's team reconstituted and re-wired morphogen signaling pathways in spatial systems to understand what features of signaling pathways enable precise spatial patterning. This work revealed specific circuit design principles underlying patterning in the Sonic Hedgehog<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Li |first1=Pulin |last2=Markson |first2=Joseph S. |last3=Wang |first3=Sheng |last4=Chen |first4=Siheng |last5=Vachharajani |first5=Vipul |last6=Elowitz |first6=Michael B. |date=2018-05-04 |title=Morphogen gradient reconstitution reveals Hedgehog pathway design principles |journal=Science |volume=360 |issue=6388 |pages=543–548 |doi=10.1126/science.aao0645 |pmc=6516753 |pmid=29622726 |bibcode=2018Sci...360..543L }}</ref> and Bone Morphogenetic Protein (BMP) pathways.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zhu |first1=Ronghui |last2=Santat |first2=Leah A. |last3=Markson |first3=Joseph S. |last4=Nandagopal |first4=Nagarajan |last5=Gregrowicz |first5=Jan |last6=Elowitz |first6=Michael B. |date=2023-07-12 |title=Reconstitution of morphogen shuttling circuits |journal=Science Advances |volume=9 |issue=28 |article-number=eadf9336 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.adf9336 |pmc=10337948 |pmid=37436981 |bibcode=2023SciA....9F9336Z }}</ref>

Elowitz's laboratory also uncovered principles of combinatorial encoding. A ubiquitous feature of cell signaling systems is their use of many-to-many interactions among sets of ligand and receptor variants. The Elowitz team showed this feature allows information to be encoded in ligand combinations and contextually decoded in different ways by different cell types.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Antebi |first1=Y. E. |last2=Linton |first2=J. M. |last3=Klumpe |first3=H. |last4=Bintu |first4=B. |last5=Gong |first5=M. |last6=Su |first6=C. |last7=McCardell |first7=R. |last8=Elowitz |first8=M. B. |title=Combinatorial Signal Perception in the BMP Pathway |journal=Cell |date=2017 |volume=170 |issue=6 |pages=1184–1196.e24 |doi=10.1016/j.cell.2017.08.015 |pmid=28886385 |pmc=5612783 }}</ref> They also worked out functional implications of this scheme in subsequent papers.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Klumpe |first1=Heidi E. |last2=Garcia-Ojalvo |first2=Jordi |last3=Elowitz |first3=Michael B. |last4=Antebi |first4=Yaron E. |date=2023-06-21 |title=The computational capabilities of many-to-many protein interaction networks |journal=Cell Systems |volume=14 |issue=6 |pages=430–446 |doi=10.1016/j.cels.2023.05.001 |pmid=37348461 |pmc=10318606 |issn=2405-4712}}</ref> The laboratory has extended this principle to systems of interacting transcription factors, showing that they could similarly provide contextual responses to combinatorial inputs.<ref>{{Cite journal |title=Contextual computation by competitive protein dimerization networks |url=https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092-8674%2825%2900105-9 |journal=Cell |volume=188 |issue=7}}</ref>

Elowitz and his team also applied synthetic biology and rewiring approaches to understand and engineer epigenetic memory, showing how cells write and maintain stable memory states at individual loci through a dynamic, stochastic system.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bintu |first1=Lacramioara |last2=Yong |first2=John |last3=Antebi |first3=Yaron E. |last4=McCue |first4=Kayla |last5=Kazuki |first5=Yasuhiro |last6=Uno |first6=Narumi |last7=Oshimura |first7=Mitsuo |last8=Elowitz |first8=Michael B. |date=2016-02-12 |title=Dynamics of epigenetic regulation at the single-cell level |journal=Science |volume=351 |issue=6274 |pages=720–724 |doi=10.1126/science.aab2956 |pmc=5108652 |pmid=26912859 |bibcode=2016Sci...351..720B }}</ref>

=== Synthetic recording systems and differentiation dynamics ===
A major challenge in biology is to recover the dynamic histories of individual cells. With Long Cai and others, the Elowitz lab developed MEMOIR, a system for recording lineage and cellular event histories within cellular genomes.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-11-21 |title=History of Cells Told Through MEMOIR |url=https://www.caltech.edu/about/news/history-cells-told-through-memoir-53041 |access-date=2026-01-14 |website=California Institute of Technology |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chow |first1=Ke-Huan K. |last2=Budde |first2=Mark W. |last3=Granados |first3=Alejandro A. |last4=Cabrera |first4=Maria |last5=Yoon |first5=Shinae |last6=Cho |first6=Soomin |last7=Huang |first7=Ting-hao |last8=Koulena |first8=Noushin |last9=Frieda |first9=Kirsten L. |last10=Cai |first10=Long |last11=Lois |first11=Carlos |last12=Elowitz |first12=Michael B. |date=2021-04-09 |title=Imaging cell lineage with a synthetic digital recording system |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.abb3099 |journal=Science |volume=372 |issue=6538 |article-number=eabb3099 |doi=10.1126/science.abb3099 |pmid=33833095 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Frieda |first1=Kirsten L. |last2=Linton |first2=James M. |last3=Hormoz |first3=Sahand |last4=Choi |first4=Joonhyuk |last5=Chow |first5=Ke-Huan K. |last6=Singer |first6=Zakary S. |last7=Budde |first7=Mark W. |last8=Elowitz |first8=Michael B. |last9=Cai |first9=Long |date=January 2017 |title=Synthetic recording and in situ readout of lineage information in single cells |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=541 |issue=7635 |pages=107–111 |doi=10.1038/nature20777 |pmid=27869821 |pmc=6487260 |bibcode=2017Natur.541..107F |issn=1476-4687}}</ref> A distinguishing feature of these systems is their ability to recover lineage information from images, preserving spatial organization.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Askary |first1=Amjad |last2=Sanchez-Guardado |first2=Luis |last3=Linton |first3=James M. |last4=Chadly |first4=Duncan M. |last5=Budde |first5=Mark W. |last6=Cai |first6=Long |last7=Lois |first7=Carlos |last8=Elowitz |first8=Michael B. |date=January 2020 |title=In situ readout of DNA barcodes and single base edits facilitated by in vitro transcription |journal=Nature Biotechnology |language=en |volume=38 |issue=1 |pages=66–75 |doi=10.1038/s41587-019-0299-4 |pmid=31740838 |pmc=6954335 |issn=1546-1696}}</ref>

Together with [[Jay Shendure]] and [[Alexander F. Schier|Alex Schier]], Elowitz co-directed the Allen Discovery Center for Cell Lineage Tracing to enable the engineering of synthetic recording systems.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Allen Discovery Center for Lineage Tracing |url=https://www.allen-lineage.org/ |access-date=2026-01-14 |website=www.allen-lineage.org}}</ref> Alongside this work, they also created and demonstrated methods for inferring cell fate programs from lineage histories.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Tran |first1=Martin |last2=Askary |first2=Amjad |last3=Elowitz |first3=Michael B. |date=2024-03-25 |title=Lineage motifs as developmental modules for control of cell type proportions |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1534580724000376 |journal=Developmental Cell |volume=59 |issue=6 |pages=812–826.e3 |doi=10.1016/j.devcel.2024.01.017 |pmid=38359830 |issn=1534-5807}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hormoz |first1=Sahand |last2=Singer |first2=Zakary S. |last3=Linton |first3=James M. |last4=Antebi |first4=Yaron E. |last5=Shraiman |first5=Boris I. |last6=Elowitz |first6=Michael B. |date=2016-11-23 |title=Inferring Cell-State Transition Dynamics from Lineage Trees and Endpoint Single-Cell Measurements |url=https://www.cell.com/fulltext/S2405-4712(16)30334-9 |journal=Cell Systems |language=English |volume=3 |issue=5 |doi=10.1016/j.cel |doi-broken-date=January 15, 2026 |issn=2405-4712 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220830165034/https://www.cell.com/fulltext/S2405-4712(16)30334-9 |archive-date=2022-08-30}}</ref>

=== Synthetic protein circuits and multicellular synthetic biology ===
The Elowitz laboratory focuses on extending synthetic biology approaches to the protein level and providing foundations for synthetic multicellular systems. For example, Elowitz and his group developed programmable protein circuits based on engineered proteases that can sense, process, and respond to signals in mammalian cells,<ref name="ReferenceA">{{Cite journal |last1=Gao |first1=Xiaojing J. |last2=Chong |first2=Lucy S. |last3=Kim |first3=Matthew S. |last4=Elowitz |first4=Michael B. |date=2018-09-21 |title=Programmable protein circuits in living cells |journal=Science |volume=361 |issue=6408 |pages=1252–1258 |doi=10.1126/science.aat5062 |pmc=7176481 |pmid=30237357 |bibcode=2018Sci...361.1252G }}</ref> or function as intracellular biochemical neural networks.<ref name="ReferenceA"/> The lab engineered other protein systems to function as RNA export systems, enabling non-destructive cell tracking, and allowing cell-to-cell transfer or delivery of mRNA.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Horns |first1=F. |last2=Martinez |first2=J. A. |last3=Fan |first3=C. |last4=Haque |first4=M. |last5=Linton |first5=J. M. |last6=Tobin |first6=V. |last7=Santat |first7=L. |last8=Maggiolo |first8=A. O. |last9=Bjorkman |first9=P. J. |last10=Lois |first10=C. |last11=Elowitz |first11=M. B. |title=Engineering RNA export for measurement and manipulation of living cells |journal=Cell |date=2023 |volume=186 |issue=17 |pages=3642–3658.e32 |doi=10.1016/j.cell.2023.06.013 |pmid=37437570 |pmc=10528933 }}</ref>

The Elowitz lab introduced "MultiFate", a synthetic circuit of engineered transcription factors that allows cells to exist in multiple stable states, and provides a foundation for engineering synthetic cell fate control.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zhu |first1=Ronghui |last2=del Rio-Salgado |first2=Jesus M. |last3=Garcia-Ojalvo |first3=Jordi |last4=Elowitz |first4=Michael B. |date=2022-01-21 |title=Synthetic multistability in mammalian cells |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.abg9765 |journal=Science |volume=375 |issue=6578 |article-number=eabg9765 |doi=10.1126/science.abg9765 |pmid=35050677 }}</ref> In related work, the lab engineered cells that could control their own population size in a mutationally robust fashion, a necessary step for synthetic multicellularity.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ma |first1=Yitong |last2=Budde |first2=Mark W. |last3=Mayalu |first3=Michaëlle N. |last4=Zhu |first4=Junqin |last5=Lu |first5=Andrew C. |last6=Murray |first6=Richard M. |last7=Elowitz |first7=Michael B. |date=2022-03-17 |title=Synthetic mammalian signaling circuits for robust cell population control |journal=Cell |language=English |volume=185 |issue=6 |pages=967–979.e12 |doi=10.1016/j.cell.2022.01.026 |issn=0092-8674 |pmid=35235768 |pmc=8995209 }}</ref>

=== Foundations for therapeutic circuits ===
A key promise of [[synthetic biology]] is the ability to rationally engineer new types of therapeutics with greater precision and specificity. To increase precision in gene therapy, the Elowitz lab developed synthetic miRNA circuits that make protein expression independent of uncontrollable variation in gene dosage.<ref name=Flynn/><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Du |first1=R. |last2=Flynn |first2=M. J. |last3=Mahe |first3=K. |last4=Honsa |first4=M. |last5=Gu |first5=B. |last6=Li |first6=D. |last7=McGeary |first7=S. E. |last8=Gradinaru |first8=V. |last9=Jungmann |first9=R. |last10=Elowitz |first10=M. B. |title=miRNA modules for precise, tunable control of gene expression |url=https://www.cell.com/molecular-cell/fulltext/S1097-2765(25)00969-4 |journal=Molecular Cell |date=2026 |volume=86 |issue=1 |pages=194–212.e7 |doi=10.1016/j.molcel.2025.11.028 |pmid=41421338 }}</ref>

The Elowitz lab has introduced therapeutic circuits — sets of engineered proteins that can be delivered as mRNA in lipid nanoparticles to selectively kill cancer cells.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Xia |first1=S. |last2=Lu |first2=A. C. |last3=Tobin |first3=V. |last4=Luo |first4=K. |last5=Moeller |first5=L. |last6=Shon |first6=D. J. |last7=Du |first7=R. |last8=Linton |first8=J. M. |last9=Sui |first9=M. |last10=Horns |first10=F. |last11=Elowitz |first11=M. B. |title=Synthetic protein circuits for programmable control of mammalian cell death |journal=Cell |date=2024 |volume=187 |issue=11 |pages=2785–2800.e16 |doi=10.1016/j.cell.2024.03.031 |pmid=38657604 |pmc=11127782 }}</ref><ref name=Lu/> By linking recognition of cancer cell state to cell killing, these circuits could help to overcome limitations with targeted therapies, such as resistance.
